title: yoga nidra
hook: at sunset the sun's rays gather back into the sun, and an Upanishad says the senses do the same at night
carry: the rays gather into the sun

segments.voice: Yesterday, yoga nidra and the sankalpa: a short, sincere resolve, said at the start and the end.

A student sits before a sage and asks a question about the body at night. When a person sleeps, what is it in them that sleeps? And what stays awake? The sage, Pippalada, answers with the evening sky. At sunset, he says, the rays of the sun all gather back into that one disc of light. At sunrise they spread out again. That's what happens to the senses every night.
screen: `WHAT SLEEPS? WHAT STAYS AWAKE?` → `THE RAYS GATHER INTO THE SUN.` → `THE SENSES GATHER IN.`

segments.voice: In the Prashna Upanishad's fourth question, a student named Gargya asks this, and Pippalada's answer, in paraphrase, is this: as the rays of the setting sun become one in its disc of light, so in sleep all the senses become one in the mind, the highest of them. Then the person doesn't hear, doesn't see, doesn't smell or taste or touch, doesn't speak or take hold or move. And people say, he sleeps. Yet the breaths, the text says, keep watch in the city of the body, like fires kept burning in a house. So sleep, here, is a gathering in. Patanjali has a name for gathering in on purpose, while awake. In the second chapter of the Yoga Sutras he calls it pratyahara: the senses withdrawing from their objects and following the mind inward. The Gita gives the picture: a tortoise drawing in its limbs. Satyananda describes yoga nidra as a way into pratyahara, and the main tool is a quick tour of the body called the rotation of awareness. The guide names a part, the right-hand thumb, the second finger, the third, the palm, the wrist, and the listener simply places attention there, without moving. Then the next part. The sense of the body begins to quiet, and the outside world thins. It looks like doing very little. But it's the senses being gathered back into the mind, the way the Upanishad saw the rays gathered into the sun, only this time on purpose.
screen: `THE SENSES BECOME ONE IN THE MIND.` · `THE BREATHS KEEP WATCH, LIKE FIRES.` · `PRATYAHARA: THE SENSES DRAWN IN.` · `ATTENTION TOURS THE BODY, PART BY PART.` · then, large: `THE RAYS GATHER INTO THE SUN.`

segments.voice: Lie down or sit back with eyes closed, and without moving, let attention go where it's named: right-hand thumb, second finger, third, fourth, fifth, palm, back of the hand, wrist, elbow, shoulder, right side of the chest, right hip, knee, ankle, right big toe. Now the whole right side, all at once. Then let attention rest on the breath, keeping watch, like a fire kept burning in a house.
Yoga nidra. The sleep of yoga, where the senses gather into the mind, like rays into the setting sun, this time on purpose.
Your line: the rays gather into the sun. Tomorrow, the one who stays awake. That's day one thousand twenty-four.

howItsDone: In guided yoga nidra, the teacher names parts of the body in a set order and listeners place attention on each without moving; teachers describe this rotation of awareness as a doorway to pratyahara, the withdrawal of the senses.

fork.setup: the guide says: right-hand thumb. what do you do?
options: wiggle it, to be sure it's there.
fork.reveal: in the rotation of awareness you simply rest attention on the part named, then move on. The senses quiet, and attention watches them gather in.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: pratyahara, the drawing in of the senses. In the Yoga Sutras, the limb of yoga before concentration.

trapdoor: what you thought: yoga nidra is just lying still and drifting off.
what it means: it gathers the senses into the mind on purpose, by touring the body with attention.
what a scholar hears: Prashna Upanishad 4.2–4.3 on sleep, and Yoga Sutra 2.54 on pratyahara.
recall: Krishna, the one with a rope at his waist

chat.says: My yoga nidra teacher just names body parts. How is that a spiritual practice?
options: It draws the senses inward, like sun rays gathering at sunset.
It's only a way to count body parts until you fall asleep.
It checks each body part for pain before deeper stretching.
chat.meaning: Satyananda calls the body tour a way into pratyahara: the senses drawn into the mind, as the Prashna's rays gather into the sun.
